content.content:
Haj-Wan: "I wait for Sei-Wan, my kin. He walked out into the basin alone, to prove himself to the Agaceph, and he has not come back. I am Agaceph too. By our custom none of us may follow a walk-out, so I stay at this gate. An outsider may follow him. He went east from the gate through the shallows, and he is up among the roots there. Vipers lie in the roots, and the mud holds anyone who stands still. Nothing that walks in the basin lives long. Gih-Xaleel, the levy warden beside me, will say the same. I want him alive. He wants the walk-out to count, and it counts only if he comes home on his own feet. If another brings him in, the Agaceph will say he did not finish. I would have him alive and shamed sooner than proud and dead. Bring him home if you must. But if he can walk, let the walk-out be his own."

input.command: /tmp/ptb-sujwgrae/play 'end' --take 'Short, clear quest. I understood who everyone was: a gate warden, a worried kinswoman, and a proud young man stuck up in the roots. The choice at the end was a good one. It was a real dilemma between respecting his pride and easing Haj-Wan'"'"'s worry, and the game did not tell me which was right. I liked that Haj-Wan'"'"'s own words hinted at the answer. Travel and combat were abstract (one command each), so there was little tension, and the viper fight was trivial. The setting is only lightly sketched, with Dwemer ruins and Agaceph customs. I would want to see more of Helstrom. Leaving Haj-Wan unaware felt slightly uncomfortable, which I think was intended. The journal ended empty of objectives, so I stopped.'

content.text:
I finished the one quest, "The Gates of Helstrom", and my journal now has no active objectives, so I ended the game.

- **The quest:** Haj-Wan, waiting at Helstrom's gate, asked me to find her kin Sei-Wan, who had walked out into the basin alone to prove himself to the Agaceph tribe. I found him up in the roots east of the gate. He wouldn't come down while a viper lay between him and home, so I killed it.
- **The choice:** I could have talked him home, which would have cost him the walk-out. Instead I told him to walk home on his own feet and said nothing at the gate. Haj-Wan still doesn't know he's safe. That felt slightly uncomfortable, but she had said to let him walk if he could.
- **What I took from it:** I told the game the quest was short and clear and the choice a real dilemma. The viper fight and travel were trivial, and the setting was only lightly sketched. I'd want to see more of Helstrom.
